title.en: Data Formats, Interfaces and Quality Checks

tagline: Move data between files, interfaces and tables without losing or corrupting it, and stop a bad batch at the boundary
description: Participants move data between files, interfaces and tables without losing or corrupting it. They compare delimited, JSON Lines and columnar files, repair encoding and time-zone faults, write a paginated API client with retries, flatten nested JSON and declare a schema whose checks stop a bad batch from loading.
audience: Beginners. Anyone starting technical data or AI work, including future analysts, data scientists, data engineers and AI engineers who can code but have not yet worked with messy real data.
prerequisites: Writes Python functions and handles exceptions (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent)

outcomes.text: Compare delimited, JSON Lines and columnar files on size, read time and type fidelity, given one dataset in each format
Explain how encodings, byte order marks and time zones corrupt data, and identify each symptom, given six damaged files
outcomes.evidence: a diagnosis correct on five of six

outcomes.text: Implement an API client that follows cursor pagination, respects rate limits, retries with backoff and keeps raw responses, given a mock API with injected errors
outcomes.evidence: a run log showing every record retrieved exactly once

outcomes.text: Convert nested JSON into typed tables written as partitioned columnar files, given the raw responses
outcomes.evidence: files whose schema matches the declared one

outcomes.text: Implement validation checks that stop a load when a batch breaks the declared schema, given batches with seeded defects
outcomes.evidence: a report that catches every defect and passes a clean batch

case_study.name: The charging network
case_study.summary: The charging network is a fictional private operator of 40 public fast-charging stations for electric vehicles in one unnamed city, whose charging sessions reach the data team as charger logs from two vendors, legacy exports from the station team and pages of the charge-point platform API. Every file is synthetic and generated with a fixed seed: 200,000 sessions for the format comparison, six damaged files, 1,200 nested sessions behind a mock API with injected faults, five batches with seeded defects, and capstone batches an assessor generates from a seed.

format_note: Workshop: two days with labs, a short pre-work task and a tracked follow-up task

days.title: Files: formats, text and time
days.subtitle: What a file promises, what it loses, and how bytes and clocks corrupt data

sessions.title: File formats
sessions.summary: Delimited dialects, JSON and JSON Lines, columnar files with partitions, and in-memory interchange, compared by measurement
outcomes: Name the dialect settings a delimited file needs: delimiter, quoting, encoding, line ending
Explain how columnar files store types, compress columns and read only what a query needs
Measure size, read time and type fidelity of one dataset in three formats

lab.title: One dataset, three formats
lab.summary: The same 200,000 charging sessions written as CSV, JSON Lines and Parquet, measured for size, read time and type fidelity, and queried with DuckDB

steps.text: Run the setup cell and generate the sessions table
Write CSV, JSON Lines and Parquet and compare their sizes
Read each file back and time it
Check type fidelity column by column
Query the Parquet file with DuckDB, and hand it an Arrow table
Write the comparison table and a recommendation

lab.stretch: Write the Parquet partitioned by day and query one partition

sessions.title: Text and time
sessions.summary: Bytes and characters, UTF-8 and legacy Arabic code pages, byte order marks, offsets, UTC and daylight saving
outcomes: Tell bytes from characters and read a file’s first bytes for its encoding
Recognise the symptom of a wrong code page, a byte order mark, double encoding and UTF-16
Convert local times without offsets to UTC, across a daylight-saving change

lab.title: Six damaged files
lab.summary: Six files from the station team and two charger vendors diagnosed from their bytes and times, repaired, checked against the platform and logged

steps.text: Run the setup cell and look at the six files as bytes
Write the diagnosis sheet, without an assistant
Repair the four text files
Convert Vendor A’s times to UTC
Convert Vendor B’s times to UTC across the clock change
Check against the platform and write the repair log

lab.stretch: Guess the code page of a file without being told

days.title: Interfaces and the boundary
days.subtitle: Pull every record exactly once, then let only a valid batch through

sessions.title: Interfaces
sessions.summary: Status codes and errors, offset and cursor pagination, rate limits, retries with backoff, raw responses, checkpoints and tokens kept out of code
outcomes: Decide from a status code whether to retry, wait or stop
Explain why cursor pagination survives inserts that offset pagination does not
Build a rerunnable pull with raw responses, a checkpoint and idempotent writes

lab.title: Every record, exactly once
lab.summary: A client for the mock charge-point platform API that follows cursors, retries with backoff, keeps raw pages and resumes from a checkpoint, then a polite pull of a public open-data API

steps.text: Run the setup cell, read the API’s terms and load the token from the environment
Fetch one page by hand: status, body and cursor
Write fetch_all: follow the cursor, keep raw pages, checkpoint
Add retries: Retry-After on 429, backoff with jitter on 5xx, stop on other errors
Interrupt the run, resume it, and prove every record arrived exactly once
Page the offset endpoint and find what it repeats and misses
Read a public open-data API’s licence, then pull every page politely

lab.stretch: Make the public pull resumable with the same checkpoint idea

sessions.title: Schema and validation
sessions.summary: Nested JSON flattened to typed tables, declared types, ranges and keys, partitioned Parquet, and failing a load versus quarantining rows
outcomes: Flatten nested records into one table per grain, keys carried down
Declare a schema and prove the written files match it
Decide per batch whether to load, quarantine rows or reject, and report why

lab.title: Flatten, write, validate
lab.summary: Raw API pages turned into typed session and reading tables written as Parquet partitioned by day, then five batches validated with JSON Schema and Pandera: loaded, quarantined or rejected

steps.text: Run the setup cell; check every raw record against the JSON Schema
Flatten the records into a sessions table and a readings table
Cast to the declared schema, write Parquet partitioned by day, check what was written
Declare the table checks with Pandera
Validate the five batches: load, quarantine or reject, and write the report
Read the quarantine file as a station owner would

lab.stretch: Add an optional field to the schema (version 2) and show that version-1 batches still pass

days.title: Live ingestion run
days.subtitle: Each participant runs the ingestion script live on a batch the assessor generates, then answers questions

examples: an Academy mock service in a container

capstone.summary: A checked ingestion script, run live on a batch the assessor supplies
capstone.submission: An individual task, submitted as a public GitHub repository link within two weeks of the workshop: the ingestion script, its declared schemas, a README with its rules and how to run it, and the report of a run on the practice batch. No token, key or .env file in the repository. The live run uses a batch the assessor generates on the day from a seed of their choice.

rubric.criterion: Every input read correctly: encodings and times normalised to UTF-8 and UTC, each repair logged
Typed, partitioned output whose written schema matches the declared one
Record and table checks applied with stated rules: load, quarantine or reject
Rerunnable: a second run on the same batch gives the same files, the input kept untouched
A report and quarantine file the data owner can act on; no token in the repository
Live run: the assessor’s batch loaded or rejected for the correct reasons, and explained
